name: Climate Physical Risk
description: The physical risks of a changing climate as they land, as they are projected, and as people respond: the trends and the major events, water, food and agriculture, insurance, property, public finance and infrastructure, from the climate desks, the agencies, the trade press and the research journals, summarized and linked.
cadence: runs with the shared routine, twice daily at 05:05 and 17:05 America/New_York; the later run is the edition for the day and earlier runs fold beneath it. Weekly sources carry longer windows so the research and attribution pieces stay in scope.
edition_size: 2 to 3 stories per subtopic, 16 to 24 at most; a subtopic with nothing significant is omitted

subtopics.name: Public finance and the financial system

subtopic_notes: Three kinds of story run in every subtopic: direct impacts (what happened, where, to whom, at what cost); projections (what the models, the insurers, the agencies and the research expect); and responses (what people do about the risk: adaptation investment, codes, hardening, retreat, and what resilience costs and who pays). An edition should carry more than one kind where the day offers them; a projection or a response ranks by what it changes.

Trends and outlooks leads the edition. A story there is about a pattern across events: the shifting baseline, records and the margin by which they fall, attribution, outlooks and reports. Major events carries single incidents at a high bar. When an event's coverage connects it to the trend, the event goes to Major events and its summary says so; an attribution study of the event goes to Trends and outlooks.

Every candidate is assigned to exactly one subtopic. A storm goes to Major events, its insured-loss estimate to Insurance and risk transfer, its federal aid to Public finance, its grid failures to Infrastructure. A drought declaration goes to Water; the same drought's crop losses go to Food and agriculture; its effect on barge traffic goes to Infrastructure. Home values and insurance-driven repricing in exposed places go to Property and communities; an insurer's withdrawal from a state goes to Insurance.
Weights are all 1.0, as in the other topics, so a later private view can reweight without changing the shape.

History. v1 (2026-10-23) had three subtopics named by the owner: weather volatility, water, economics. v2 and v3 (2026-10-25) were vocabulary only. v4 (2026-10-25) follows the owner's read of five days of editions, 33 stories: weather too episodic, economics only the surface. Weather volatility split into Trends and outlooks and Major events; Economics split into Insurance, Property, Public finance and Infrastructure; Food and agriculture added; responses added as a third story kind. Stories filed before v4 keep their old subtopics, weather-volatility and economics.

Decisions taken as the session's recommendations on 2026-10-25, open to the owner's revision: the eight subtopics; food and agriculture in; responses as a story kind; caps of three per subtopic; geography global with U.S. depth where the reporting is; Google News search feeds admitted as signal for the thinnest subtopics, since the coverage step resolves their headlines by search; the cadence and the page role unchanged.
deprioritize: energy transition, emissions and net-zero stories without a physical-impact or physical-risk angle
climate negotiations and climate politics, unless they change how physical risk is financed or insured
insurance lines unrelated to catastrophe and property: auto, liability, workers' compensation, life, health
insurer quarterly earnings that move neither pricing nor capacity
routine procedural items from water agencies (meeting agendas, comment periods, staff reports) without an allocation, restriction, or shortage decision
farm policy, trade and tariff stories without a weather or climate cause
housing-market, mortgage-rate and freight-rate stories without a hazard or climate angle
state and local government stories unrelated to disasters, climate costs or climate risk
monetary policy and central-bank speeches that do not address climate or physical risk
single-event weather coverage with no toll, cost, record, or projection attached

coverage.discovery_note: No web-search discovery, as in the other topics. Google News search feeds, left out at launch because their links cannot be read, were admitted in v4 as signal for three thin subtopics; the coverage step searches each headline.

editorial.summary_rule: original prose, written from coverage the agent read; no verbatim passages beyond a short attributed quote. Where a story carries a number (a toll, a loss estimate, an allocation, a projected change, a price), the number and its source are the point; keep them. For a response story, say what it costs and who pays where the coverage says.

subtopic_scope_notes.trends-and-outlooks: The shifting baseline: changes in frequency and intensity, records and the margin by which they fall, attribution studies, El Niño and seasonal outlooks, ocean heat and sea-level rise, monthly and annual climate reports, model projections, tipping-point research. The lead subtopic. NOAA's outlooks and reports now arrive through its news feed; the WMO and Copernicus still arrive only through the desks that cover them.
subtopic_scope_notes.major-events: Single events at a high bar: a record, a large toll or loss, or a precedent (a first, or outside the historical range). Three at most. Where the coverage connects the event to the trend, the summary says so. A storm with neither toll, record nor precedent is left out, however much coverage it has.
subtopic_scope_notes.water: Restrictions, rationing, allocations, shortages, aquifer and reservoir levels, snowpack, and the litigation and agreements that divide water, worldwide with the U.S. West in depth because that is where the reporting is; and the projections: basin forecasts, groundwater studies, availability under warming. A restriction or allocation decision outranks a report about one. Unchanged from v3.
subtopic_scope_notes.food-and-agriculture: Yields and crop failures, commodity price shocks (cocoa, coffee, olive oil, rice export bans), livestock and heat, soil and land degradation, crop insurance and farm credit, and the farm adaptations that respond to them. Farm policy and trade stories without a weather or climate cause are out.
subtopic_scope_notes.insurance: Losses, withdrawals and rate actions, reinsurance pricing, catastrophe bonds and parametric cover, protection gaps. Insurer quarterly earnings are out unless they move pricing or capacity. Capped at three so the trade press, which publishes most, does not fill the edition.
subtopic_scope_notes.property-and-communities: Where risk meets where people live: home values and mortgage risk in exposed places, insurance-driven repricing, flood maps and building codes, buyouts and managed retreat, climate migration and displacement. Housing-market stories without a climate or hazard angle are out.
subtopic_scope_notes.public-finance: Who carries what insurance does not: disaster aid and FEMA, state and municipal budgets and credit ratings, sovereign debt and disaster clauses; and the financial system's view of physical risk: central-bank and supervisor stress tests, bank and asset-manager exposure, disclosure rules, how bond and equity markets price it. A single disaster declaration or aid approval runs only when it is large or sets a precedent.
subtopic_scope_notes.infrastructure: The operating economy: power grids under heat and storms, wildfire and utility liability, transport chokepoints (the Panama Canal, the Rhine, the Mississippi), ports, industrial water for chips and data centers, business interruption, heat and labor productivity. Logistics, freight-rate and tariff stories without a weather or climate cause are out.

source_roles.agenda: Sets what is significant today. Eight desks: the Guardian's extreme weather, climate crisis, water and farming feeds; NYT Climate; Carbon Brief; Circle of Blue; Artemis; Insurance Journal; FT Climate Capital; Inside Climate News.
source_roles.signal: Corroborates and widens the aperture, and carries the projections and most of the new subtopics: the agencies and research sources, the regional water press, the reinsurance trade press, the farm, housing, state-government, utility and shipping press, and three Google News searches. Items are candidates like any other, judged on consequence; a story only these feeds surfaced is the measure of what the agenda missed.
